"You look for the assumption that makes a problem slow, or makes extra compute buy only more of the same. Ask which part
of the work waits on another part, and whether it must. Ask which quantity is measured, and whether a different but
related quantity would be cheaper to compute, easier to split, or more informative. Ask whether the unit of work is the
right one, or whether the work could be cut, merged or reordered. Ask whether the objective is the right one: the single
best answer, a ranking, a distribution, a rare tail, or a yes or no. Ask what is held fixed that need not be. Prefer
changes that alter what more compute buys over changes that only run the same work more times.

Here is a research problem as it was first written down, with the question it belongs to.
Root question: What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?
Problem:
Inference-time steering of VLA internals (SAEs, FFN vectors, conceptors, linear observers)
Steering a VLA's internal features can bring out behaviour the model already has, without retraining. On real DROID hardware, SAE steering of pi0.5 raised target-object grasps by +9 to +21 out of 25 trials, and ablating the top-4 general features cut success from 39/40 to 0/40. COAST conceptors raised pi0.5 on LIBERO-10 from 0.43 to 0.80, with about +40% on three real tasks. Grant et al. found motor programs bound to absolute coordinates (50/50 grasps at the recorded spot on a UR10e). All tests are rigid tabletop tasks; none is cloth or a dish rack. Goodfire markets steering for robotics but publishes no numbers.
What more compute would buy: The quantity is closed-loop rollouts and SAEs swept; the largest is 420,000+ rollouts and 520+ SAEs across six VLAs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19233), and above that it is unknown whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour, because every sweep so far ran rigid pick-and-place or drawer tasks.
What runs step after step: Each feature waits on an SAE fit (about 6,700 Adam steps, derived from https://arxiv.org/html/2603.19183; 'a few GPU-hours per SAE on one A100') and then on closed-loop rollouts of up to 300 steps, each waiting on a ~150 ms VLA forward pass and the next observation; the answer needed 150 rollouts × 135 features (20,250 episodes), and one unbatched rollout leaves the GPU idle while the simulator steps. Steps within a rollout must run in order, but rollouts are independent: batching hundreds of steered environments in a GPU-parallel simulator, with a separate hook per environment and simulation pipelined against inference, would run them together; this pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth). The nearest attempt is RLinf-VLA, 1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill environments, for RL rather than interpretability (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06710v2).

Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then look for reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective or the order of steps that would let more compute change the answer. Give up to three. End each with one question someone could investigate: specific, answerable by a measurement, and naming what is measured. For each, give the cheapest measurement that would answer it or show it is not worth pursuing, with a rough cost. Decide from the text above and what you know; do not use tools.

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:
{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"reframes\"],\"properties\":{\"reframes\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"bottleneck\",\"assumption\",\"reframe\",\"question\",\"measure\",\"compute_after\",\"exact\",\"expected\",\"fails_if\",\"closest_prior\"],\"properties\":{\"bottleneck\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"assumption\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"reframe\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"question\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"measure\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"compute_after\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"exact\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"expected\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"fails_if\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"closest_prior\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}}}}}"

Let me carefully analyze this problem.

The problem is about inference-time steering of VLA (Vision-Language-Action) model internals using SAEs, FFN vectors, conceptors, linear observers. The stated bottleneck:

- Each feature evaluation waits on: (1) an SAE fit (~6,700 Adam steps, a few GPU-hours per SAE on one A100), then (2) closed-loop rollouts up to 300 steps, each step waiting on ~150ms VLA forward pass + next observation.
- The answer needed 150 rollouts × 135 features = 20,250 episodes.
- One unbatched rollout leaves GPU idle while simulator steps.
- Steps within a rollout must run in order, but rollouts are independent.
- All tests are rigid tabletop tasks; none is cloth or dish rack. The key open question: does any feature control contact-rich or deformable behaviour? Unknown because every sweep ran rigid pick-and-place or drawer tasks.
- Batching hundreds of steered environments pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth).

So where does compute stop helping / buy more of the same?

1. **The measured quantity is per-feature success rate on rigid tasks.** More rollouts on rigid pick-and-place only buys tighter estimates of a quantity that doesn't answer the actual question (contact-rich/deformable control). The sim-to-real gap for cloth means more simulated rollouts buy nothing real. The reframe: instead of measuring "success rate per feature," measure something cheaper and more informative — e.g., measure the causal effect of a feature on an intermediate quantity that transfers, like contact force distribution, or measure feature effect on the policy's action distribution in a few states (open-loop perturbation response) rather than closed-loop rollouts. Actually the prompt hints: "Ask which quantity is measured, and whether a different but related quantity would be cheaper to compute, easier to split, or more informative."

2. **The unit of work: one rollout per feature, sequential within rollout.** Reframe: instead of evaluating features one at a time with 150 rollouts each, use the structure: many features can be screened with a cheap open-loop metric (e.g., change in predicted action on a fixed dataset of states — a "counterfactual action divergence" measured in a single batched forward pass over a held-out dataset). Then only top features get closed-loop rollouts. This changes what compute buys: screening 135 features becomes a batched forward-pass job (massively parallel, no sequential dependence), and rollouts are spent only on the tail.

3. **The objective: binary success (yes/no at end of 300 steps).** A yes/no needs many trials to estimate (binomial variance). A continuous, per-step quantity — e.g., distance-to-goal reduction, grasp quality score, or a learned reward/value — has lower variance per rollout, so fewer rollouts are needed; or a ranking objective rather than estimating each feature's absolute success. Also: adaptive/bandit allocation (sequential hypothesis testing, best-arm identification) instead of fixed 150 rollouts per feature — early-stop features that are clearly dead. Fixed 150×135 = 20,250 regardless of signal; most features do nothing, so compute is wasted confirming zeros. Best-arm identification changes what more compute buys: compute concentrates on the informative comparisons.

4. **What is held fixed that need not be:** The SAE itself is fit once per model (6,700 Adam steps), then each feature is evaluated. But actually the pipeline is: fit SAE → steer each of 135 features → rollouts. The assumption that you need a fitted SAE per feature before any rollout. Alternative: skip SAE fitting; search directly in activation space with unsupervised directions (PCA, random directions, or gradient-free search over steering vectors evaluated by cheap metric). Or: the SAE fit is a per-model cost; sweeping 520 SAEs across six VLAs is brute force. Could fit one SAE on pooled activations? Hmm.

5. **Sim-to-real for cloth:** The key assumption is that steering effects in simulation match real robot; false for cloth. So more compute on simulated cloth rollouts buys nothing. Reframe: measure the steering effect as a delta in a representation that transfers — e.g., measure effect on latent action chunks / feature activations rather than task success, and check whether the *direction* of effect (in action space) is preserved between sim and real on a small number of real rollouts. I.e., change the objective from "success rate in sim" to "rank correlation of feature effects between sim and real" — a small real-robot study (say 5 features × 20 rollouts = 100 real episodes) determines whether sim sweeps are worth scaling at all. This is a great reframe: the quantity measured becomes a correlation/transfer coefficient, cheap, and decides whether the 20,250-episode sim sweeps should be run at all.

Let me pick the best three reframes:

**Reframe 1: Change the measured quantity from closed-loop success to open-loop action divergence (screening metric).**
- Bottleneck: 20,250 sequential closed-loop rollouts, each up to 300 steps × 150ms.
- Assumption: a feature's relevance must be measured by task success in closed loop.
- Reframe: measure the counterfactual change in the policy's action output when the feature is steered, on a fixed batch of recorded states from the target domain (including cloth/dish-rack demos). This is a pure forward-pass job: batch thousands of (state, steering) pairs, no sequential dependence, GPU fully utilized. Then only the top-k features by divergence get closed-loop rollouts.
- Question: "Does open-loop action-divergence on recorded cloth/dish states rank features the same as closed-loop success rate on the subset where both are measured?" — measured by Spearman rank correlation between the two rankings over, say, 30 features.
- Cheapest measurement: take an existing pi0.5 setup, one SAE, 30 features, DROID/LIBERO replay states; compute divergence in one batched run (~hours on one GPU), and 30 features × 50 rollouts = 1,500 closed-loop episodes for ground truth (~at 150ms × 300 steps = 45s/episode ≈ 19 GPU-hours unbatched, less batched). Rough cost: single-digit GPU-days.
- compute_after: if correlation is high, screening becomes O(features × dataset forward passes) — embarrassingly parallel — and rollouts drop from 150/feature to a handful for the top few; more compute then buys coverage of all 520 SAEs rather than 135 features.
- exact: Spearman ρ between open-loop divergence ranking and closed-loop success-delta ranking across 30 features on 3 tasks.
- expected: ρ ≈ 0.5–0.8 based on the fact that ablation of top-4 features already wipes out behaviour (39/40 → 0/40), meaning large effects are visible in action space.
- fails_if: steering effects are primarily compounding/closed-loop (contact feedback) so open-loop divergence doesn't predict success; then ρ ≈ 0 and the reframe fails — especially likely for contact-rich cloth, which is exactly the case that matters.
- closest_prior: open-loop action-divergence / "counterfactual action" probes; Grant et al.'s coordinate-binding finding used held-out replay-style evaluation; also standard SAE "feature effect" dashboards measure logit effects open-loop (like Goodfire/Anthropic feature dashboards measure activation→output effects without rollouts).

**Reframe 2: Change the objective/allocation from fixed 150 rollouts per feature to sequential best-arm identification (bandit).**
- Bottleneck: most of the 135 features do nothing; 150 rollouts each confirm zeros. Binomial yes/no success needs large n.
- Assumption: each feature needs the same fixed number of rollouts, and success must be estimated per feature rather than finding the few that matter.
- Reframe: treat feature selection as best-arm identification / successive rejects: allocate rollouts adaptively, early-stop features whose effect is statistically bounded near zero; also replace binary success with a per-step progress score (lower variance per rollout) to shrink required n.
- Question: "How many rollouts does successive-rejects need to recover the same top-5 feature set as the fixed 150×135 sweep, and what fraction of compute does it save?" measured by rollout count to identify the same top-5 with 95% confidence.
- Cheapest measurement: replay the existing 20,250-episode logs (or re-run in sim) and simulate the bandit allocation offline on recorded outcomes — cost is CPU-hours, essentially free if logs exist; if not, one sim sweep of ~20k batched episodes (with 256 parallel envs at RLinf-VLA 1.6–1.9× throughput, ~ tens of GPU-hours).
- compute_after: compute concentrates on the informative tail; more compute buys deeper feature libraries (thousands of features) rather than uniform noise reduction.
- exact: number of episodes to identify top-5 features (by success delta) with probability ≥0.95 under successive rejects vs fixed allocation, on recorded sweep data.
- expected: 3–10× episode reduction, because effect sizes are bimodal (top-4 ablation kills behaviour; most features null).
- fails_if: effects are small and uniform (many features each worth +1–2%), so no early stopping is possible and adaptivity saves little.
- closest_prior: successive rejects / UCB best-arm identification (Audibert et al.); adaptive evaluation in LLM benchmarks (e.g., adaptivehelm); RLinf-VLA for batched rollouts.

**Reframe 3: Change what is measured from sim success to sim-to-real effect-size correlation (decide whether sim sweeps are worth scaling at all) — especially for cloth/deformable.**
- Bottleneck: above 420k rollouts / 520 SAEs it's unknown whether any feature controls contact-rich/deformable behaviour, because all sweeps ran rigid tasks; and sim steering effects don't transfer for cloth, so more sim rollouts buy more of the same (precise estimates of a non-transferring quantity).
- Assumption: the path to cloth/dish tasks is to run bigger sweeps in simulation; sim is a faithful proxy.
- Reframe: change the objective to measuring the transfer coefficient itself: for a handful of features, measure the steering effect (action divergence and success delta) in both sim and real, and estimate the rank correlation of feature effects across the sim–real boundary. This is a small, decisive experiment that gates whether any large sim sweep on deformable tasks should happen.
- Question: "What is the Spearman correlation between per-feature steering effects (success-rate delta) measured in a deformable-object simulator and on the real robot for the same N features?" — measured on, e.g., 10 features × 30 sim + 30 real rollouts on one cloth task (towel fold) and one dish-rack task.
- Cheapest measurement: 10 features × 30 real episodes × 2 tasks = 600 real episodes (~at 3–5 min/episode with resets ≈ 30–50 robot-hours, one robot ~1–2 weeks) plus batched sim (~tens of GPU-hours). Real-robot time dominates; cost ~ a few thousand dollars of operator/robot time.
- compute_after: if correlation is high, sim compute becomes valuable — scale to thousands of features batched; if low, redirect compute to real-world rollouts with bandit allocation (reframe 2) or to open-loop real replay (reframe 1).
- exact: Spearman ρ between sim and real per-feature success deltas across 10 features × 2 tasks; ρ̂ with bootstrap CI.
- expected: ρ moderate for rigid tasks (known ~transferable, given +9 to +21 real gains from SAE steering match sim screening), unknown/possibly ~0 for cloth.
- fails_if: the variance of the real estimate at 30 episodes/feature swamps the correlation — with binary success and 30 episodes, standard error ~0.09, so features with deltas <0.2 are indistinguishable; if true effects are small, the measurement is underpowered and should switch to continuous progress scores.
- closest_prior: sim-vs-real policy evaluation correlation studies (e.g., "sim2real predictivity" work, Kadian et al. SIMPAR "Sim2Real Predictivity" 2019); RLinf-VLA notes steering-sim matching real is false for cloth.

These three are solid. Now let me also double check the schema requires fields: bottleneck, assumption, reframe, question, measure, compute_after, exact, expected, fails_if, closest_prior. All strings.

Let me write concise but specific strings.

Reframe 1:
- bottleneck: "20,250 closed-loop rollouts (150 × 135 features), each up to 300 sequential steps at ~150 ms per forward pass; the GPU idles between steps and every feature pays the full rollout cost regardless of effect size."
- assumption: "A feature's value can only be measured by closed-loop task success, so every candidate feature must be paid for in full episodes."
- reframe: "Screen features open-loop: measure the counterfactual change in the policy's predicted action chunk when each feature is steered, over a fixed batch of recorded states (including cloth/dish-rack demonstrations). This converts per-feature evaluation from a sequential 300-step episode into one batched forward pass over (state, steering) pairs; only the top-k by divergence get closed-loop rollouts."
- question: "Does the ranking of features by open-loop steered action-divergence on recorded states match the ranking by closed-loop success-rate delta, measured as Spearman ρ over ~30 features on 3 tasks?"
- measure: "Fit/reuse one SAE on pi0.5; compute L2 divergence of predicted action chunks for 30 steering directions over ~10k replay states (one batched run, ~2–5 GPU-hours on one A100) and get ground truth from 30 features × 50 rollouts = 1,500 episodes (~15–25 GPU-hours batched in ManiSkill/LIBERO). Total ≈ 1–2 GPU-days."
- compute_after: "If ρ is high, screening 520 SAEs × thousands of features becomes a pure forward-pass workload — embarrassingly parallel across GPUs — and rollout budget is spent only on the top few features; more compute buys feature coverage, not repeated episodes."
- exact: "Spearman ρ between open-loop action-chunk divergence ranking and closed-loop success-delta ranking across 30 features × 3 tasks, with bootstrap CI."
- expected: "ρ ≈ 0.5–0.8: ablating just the top-4 general features already collapses success (39/40 → 0/40), so large steering effects are visible directly in action space."
- fails_if: "Steering effects are dominated by closed-loop contact feedback (compounding errors only visible at step 200+), so open-loop divergence on replay states is uncorrelated with success — most likely exactly for cloth and dish-rack contact, the cases that matter."
- closest_prior: "Standard SAE feature-effect dashboards (logit/activation effects measured without rollouts, e.g., Goodfire/Anthropic-style), and Grant et al.'s replay-based probe that found motor programs bound to absolute coordinates on a UR10e."

Reframe 2:
- bottleneck: "A fixed 150 rollouts per feature spends most of the 20,250 episodes confirming null effects; binary success at step 300 is the highest-variance quantity available, forcing large n."
- assumption: "Every feature must get an equal, pre-committed rollout budget and the objective must be an estimate of each feature's success rate."
- reframe: "Change the objective from 'estimate every feature's success rate' to 'find the few features that matter': best-arm identification (successive rejects / UCB) with early elimination, and replace binary end-of-episode success with a per-step progress score (distance-to-goal / grasp-quality), which has lower variance per rollout and shrinks the n needed for each comparison."
- question: "How many episodes does successive-rejects allocation need to recover the same top-5 features as the fixed 150×135 sweep with ≥95% probability, and what is the episode savings factor?"
- measure: "Answer offline by replaying existing sweep logs (or a one-time 20k-episode sim sweep at RLinf-VLA-style 1.6–1.9× throughput with 256 envs, ~tens of GPU-hours) and simulating the bandit allocation on recorded outcomes — CPU-hours if logs exist."
- compute_after: "Rollout compute concentrates on the informative tail; more compute then buys deeper feature libraries (10× more features) instead of uniform confidence intervals on zeros."
- exact: "Episodes-to-top-5 at P(correct) ≥ 0.95 under successive rejects vs fixed allocation, measured on recorded sweep outcomes; also variance comparison of binary success vs per-step progress score."
- expected: "3–10× episode reduction, because the effect distribution is bimodal (top-4 ablation alone kills behaviour; most features do nothing), which is the regime where best-arm identification wins most."
- fails_if: "Steering effects are many, small and uniform (+1–2% each across dozens of features), so no arm can be eliminated early and adaptive allocation saves little over the fixed budget."
- closest_prior: "Successive-rejects / UCB best-arm identification (Audibert, Bubeck, Munos 2010); adaptive-subsampling LLM evaluation; RLinf-VLA (1.61–1.88× with 256 ManiSkill envs) supplies the batched-rollout substrate."

Reframe 3:
- bottleneck: "Above 420k rollouts and 520 SAEs it is still unknown whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour, because every sweep ran rigid pick-and-place/drawer tasks — and where sim steering does not match the real robot (false for cloth), each additional simulated rollout buys a tighter estimate of a quantity that does not transfer: more of the same."
- assumption: "The path to cloth and dish-rack steering is to scale simulation sweeps; i.e., feature effects found in sim transfer to real hardware."
- reframe: "Change the measured quantity from 'success rate in sim' to the transfer coefficient itself: for a small set of features, estimate each one's steering effect (success-rate delta) in both a deformable simulator and on real hardware, and measure the cross-domain rank correlation. This gates whether any large deformable sim sweep should be run at all."
- question: "What is the Spearman correlation between per-feature steering effects measured in a deformable sim and on the real robot, over ~10 features on one cloth task (towel fold) and one dish-rack task?"
- measure: "10 features × 30 episodes × 2 tasks × 2 domains: 600 batched sim episodes (a few GPU-hours with parallel envs) and 600 real episodes (~3–5 min each with resets ≈ 40–50 robot-hours, i.e., ~1–2 weeks on one DROID-class arm, a few thousand dollars of operator time). Real time dominates."
- compute_after: "If ρ is high, sim compute becomes worth scaling to thousands of features; if ρ ≈ 0, compute redirects to real-world rollouts with bandit allocation (reframe 2) or real replay-state screening (reframe 1), and no GPU sim sweep on cloth is run."
- exact: "Spearman ρ (with bootstrap CI) between sim and real per-feature success deltas across 10 features × 2 tasks; report per-task."
- expected: "ρ moderate-to-high for the rigid dish-rack adjacent components (consistent with the +9 to +21 real gains achieved from sim-screened SAE steering on DROID hardware), unknown and possibly near 0 for cloth."
- fails_if: "At 30 real episodes per feature, the binomial standard error (~0.09) exceeds the true effect sizes, so the correlation estimate is noise-dominated; then switch the measured quantity to a continuous per-step progress score or more episodes before concluding anything."
- closest_prior: "Sim2Real predictivity studies that measure sim-vs-real policy-rank correlation (Kadian et al., SIMPAR 2019); the problem text itself notes the known failure that sim steering effects do not match real for cloth; RLinf-VLA as batched-sim substrate."
